title: Appeals Court Skeptical of Federal Bid to Block 20,000 California Ballots
snippet: A 9th Circuit panel questioned both the constitutionality and jurisdiction behind the Justice Department's emergency request to force California election officials to set aside thousands of votes.
content:
A federal appeals court panel voiced deep skepticism on Sunday over a last-minute attempt by the Justice Department to force California election officials to isolate 20,000 ballots over unverified citizenship concerns.

During a rare weekend emergency hearing, judges on the U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals questioned whether the federal government even has the constitutional authority or legal standing to intervene in state election administration just days before voting concludes.

Constitutional and Jurisdictional Hurdles

Judge Mark J. Bennett, an appointee of President Trump, repeatedly challenged Justice Department attorney Matthew Donnelly on how the administration’s request aligns with the U.S. Constitution's Elections Clause, which grants states primary authority over election procedures.

"It seems to me that you want us to issue an injunction that is entirely inconsistent with the law the California Legislature has adopted pursuant to the Elections Clause," Bennett said during the hour-long hearing. "How can we do that?"

Bennett also questioned why the appellate court was hearing the emergency appeal before the lower district court judge had issued a formal ruling or conducted fact-finding on the matter, calling the court's jurisdiction into doubt.

Disputed Data and Potential Election Disruption

The Justice Department sought an emergency injunction requiring California Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder Dean Logan to halt the counting of 20,000 flagged voters until their citizenship status could be verified. DOJ attorneys claimed to possess evidence that ineligible noncitizens were registered on state rolls.

However, attorneys representing California emphasized that the federal government's list relied on flawed third-party data sets. State officials noted that preliminary reviews of the flagged list revealed native-born U.S. citizens and individuals who were not even registered to vote.

Judge Gabriel P. Sanchez, an appointee of President Biden, repeatedly pressed the Justice Department on the origin and reliability of its voter list, which Donnelly could not fully explain. California Deputy Solicitor General Samuel P. Siegel urged the court to throw out the appeal for lack of jurisdiction, warning that forcing state officials to re-segregate processed ballots would cause severe disruption to the ongoing election.

Broad Context of Election Challenges

The third panel member, Judge Patrick J. Bumatay, also a Trump appointee, focused his questioning on how states should handle allegations of illegal noncitizen voting. State attorneys responded that established statutory procedures already exist to handle voter challenges, requiring strict evidentiary standards that federal prosecutors failed to meet.

Legal scholars and voting rights advocates noted that the Justice Department's emergency request strays from long-held federal policies prohibiting major election interventions close to voting deadlines. With millions of ballots already cast in California, the court is expected to issue a decision swiftly.
